A_target.statement:
Let $\map P n$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|propositional function]] on $\N$ such that:
:$\forall k \in \N: \paren {\forall j < k: \map P j} \implies \map P k$
Then $\map P n$ holds for all $n \in \N$.

B_source.statement: Every [[Definition:Non-Empty Set|non-empty]] subset of $\N$ has a [[Definition:Smallest Element|smallest element]].

derived.P(j) for all j<m: the hypothesis then forces P(m), contradicting m in S

object_map.reformulation: Recast 'prove P for all n' as 'the set of counterexamples is empty', then invoke well-ordering on that set (proof by minimal counterexample).

validity_conditions: Let S be the set of n with P(n) false; suppose S nonempty.
Well-ordering gives a least m in S, so P(j) holds for all j < m.
The strong-induction hypothesis then yields P(m), contradicting m in S; hence S is empty.
proof_plan: Assume the premise, and {{AimForCont}} that $\map P n$ fails for some $n$.
Let $S = \set {n \in \N: \neg \map P n}$, which is non-empty.
By the [[Well-Ordering Principle]], $S$ has a least element $m$.

For all $j < m$, $j \notin S$, so $\map P j$ holds.
By the premise $\map P m$ holds, contradicting $m \in S$.
Hence $\map P n$ holds for all $n$, which is the [[Second Principle of Mathematical Induction]].
{{qed}}
